meta.title: Who really said "Famous for being famous"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Andy Warhol. The phrase is in print in 1896, in Charles Godfrey Leland's Legends of Florence — critics applied it to Warhol in 1974.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Famous for being famous'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Andy Warhol. The phrase appears in 1896 in Leland's Legends of Florence; Boorstin popularized the idea in 1962. Critics pinned it on Warhol.

answer.label: Not Andy Warhol — critics said it about him
answer.sourceLine: Warhol did not coin this — it was a phrase other people used to describe him. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ finds “famous for being famous” already in print in its modern sense in 1896, in Charles Godfrey Leland’s Legends of Florence, Second Series — before Warhol was born — and again in Hans Otto Storm’s novel Count Ten in 1940. Daniel J. Boorstin popularised the idea in 1962 with different words. The earliest Warhol link QI documents is a January 1974 Guardian review that applies the phrase to him.

source.heading: The earliest documented use

docMeta.dd: Legends of Florence, Collected from the People and Re-told by Charles Godfrey Leland (Hans Breitmann), Second Series
“La Via del Gomitolo del Oro, and How it got its Name”
1896 — Macmillan & Co., New York; David Nutt, London

source.excerpt: To which the observant Flaxius appends: “There are in the world, of women not a few, and many men, I ween, well thereunto, whose whole life and highest aim is really not to win gold for real pleasure, or even for avarice or aught solid, but merely to live in its glitter and sheen — to frôler and froisser, rumple and rustle drap d’or and damask drapery, jingle jewels, in a kind of fade ostentation, as doth a professional beauty or an actress famous for being famous, nothing more, and being diamonded or demi-monded for famousness…”
trail: 1896 — Charles Godfrey Leland uses it of “an actress famous for being famous, nothing more” on page 229 of Legends of Florence, Second Series (full text at the Internet Archive ↗).
1962 — Daniel J. Boorstin gives the idea its enduring form in The Image: “The celebrity is a person who is known for his well-knownness” (transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗).
31 January 1974 — The Guardian’s John Coleman, reviewing Stephen Koch’s Stargazer, writes of Warhol: “Famous for being famous, he is pure image” — the earliest Warhol connection QI documents ↗.
Today — the line circulates under Warhol’s name, though it appears nowhere among his sourced quotations on Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Internet Archive scan of the 1896 David Nutt (London) printing at page 229; Quote Investigator verified the same passage at page 229 of the Macmillan (New York) printing. Flaxius is the commenting figure Leland uses to close his Florentine legends.

sourceLink.text: Read Legends of Florence, Second Series (1896) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The excerpt above is from Leland’s Legends of Florence, Second Series, first published in 1896 — comfortably before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the United States and free to quote. Later formulations of the same idea are not: Boorstin’s The Image (1962) and the 1974 Guardian review remain in copyright to their authors and publishers, so only short quotation of those is appropriate.

author.name: Charles Godfrey Leland
author.heading: The man who wrote it first
author.bio: Charles Godfrey Leland was an American humorist and folklorist, best known in his own lifetime as the author of the comic Hans Breitmann’s Ballads (1871). He spent his later years in Europe collecting folk tales, publishing Legends of Florence, Collected from the People in 1896 and the witchcraft text Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches. The four words that would later define modern celebrity appear almost in passing in his 1896 Florentine collection — a stray jab at “an actress famous for being famous, nothing more.”

cite.sourceCitation: Charles Godfrey Leland, “La Via del Gomitolo del Oro, and How it got its Name,” in Legends of Florence, Collected from the People and Re-told by Charles Godfrey Leland (Hans Breitmann), Second Series (London: David Nutt, 1896), 229. Earliest documented use of the phrase in its modern sense per Quote Investigator, which verified the same passage at page 229 of the Macmillan (New York) printing.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: Three names attach themselves to these four words. Only one of them is documented as having put the phrase into print first, and it is not the famous one.

items.tag: Said about him, not by him
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states plainly that the saying is linked to Warhol because it was often applied to him, and cites The Guardian of 31 January 1974 — John Coleman reviewing Stephen Koch’s Stargazer — writing of Warhol: “Famous for being famous, he is pure image.” Wikiquote’s page of his sourced quotations ↗ does not contain the phrase at all.

Boorstin’s The Image (1962) is where the modern concept took hold, but his actual wording ↗ was “The celebrity is a person who is known for his well-knownness,” alongside “notorious for their notoriety” and “well known for its well-knownness.” QI credits him with popularising the notion, not with the four-word phrase.

items.tag: Often called the first — he wasn't
items.why: Wikipedia ↗ says Muggeridge “may have been the first to use the actual phrase,” in the 1967 introduction to Muggeridge Through The Microphone: “Today one is famous for being famous.” But QI’s chronology ↗ documents the phrase in print in 1896 and again in 1940.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: Charles Godfrey Leland employed the phrase “famous for being famous” with the modern sense in 1896; Hans Otto Storm used it again in 1940; and Daniel J. Boorstin popularised the notion in 1962 with The Image. Warhol’s name arrived last, attached by other people’s pens.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Warhol
lead: Warhol was not the author of the phrase; he was its best illustration. By the mid-1970s critics reached for “famous for being famous” whenever they needed to explain an artist whose principal medium seemed to be his own visibility. The line and the man fused, and a description hardened into a quotation.

There is a second layer to the irony. Even Warhol’s genuinely signature line about fame — the fifteen-minutes prophecy that Wikiquote traces to a 1968 Stockholm exhibition catalogue — is contested ↗, with curator Pontus Hultén, photographer Nat Finkelstein and painter Larry Rivers all named as possible sources. Warhol is, in the most literal sense, quoted for being quoted.
context.detailsSummary: More stops on the phrase’s route
detailsBody: Quote Investigator records the actress Raquel Welch using the line about herself in The Los Angeles Times in 1966: “I am famous for being famous.”

In July 1967 an Indianapolis columnist applied it to Jayne Mansfield and Zsa Zsa Gabor; in 1970 LIFE applied it to Oscar Wilde; and in April 1974 the newsman David Brinkley turned it on his own trade in The Washington Post: “Mainly, he is famous for being famous.”
By 2004 it had been absorbed into the reference shelf ↗: The Oxford Dictionary of Idioms gives it an entry, glossed as “having no recognizable reason for your fame other than high media exposure.”
context.pull: “Famous for being famous, he is pure image.” — The Guardian on Warhol, 31 January 1974

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's chronology documents 'famous for being famous' in Leland's Legends of Florence (1896) and Storm's Count Ten (1940); credits Boorstin's The Image (1962) with popularizing the notion via 'known for his well-knownness'; states the saying is linked to Andy Warhol because it was often applied to him, quoting The Guardian of 31 January 1974 (John Coleman on Stephen Koch's Stargazer): 'Famous for being famous, he is pure image.' Also records Raquel Welch 1966, an Indianapolis columnist July 1967, LIFE 1970, David Brinkley in The Washington Post April 1974, and the 2004 Oxford Dictionary of Idioms entry.

The 1896 Legends of Florence, Second Series contains, at page 229 in the chapter 'La Via del Gomitolo del Oro, and How it got its Name', the Flaxius passage reading 'as doth a professional beauty or an actress famous for being famous, nothing more, and being diamonded or demi-monded for famousness'. Item metadata: creator 'Leland, Charles Godfrey, 1824-1903', date 1896, publisher 'London, Nutt', volume '2, ser.2'.

Wikipedia traces the term to Daniel J. Boorstin's The Image (1962), 'a person who is known for his well-knownness', and says Malcolm Muggeridge 'may have been the first to use the actual phrase' in the 1967 introduction to Muggeridge Through The Microphone: 'Today one is famous for being famous.' The article does not credit Andy Warhol with the phrase.

Wikiquote's Andy Warhol page (sections: Quotes by decade, undated quotes, Quotes about Andy Warhol, External links) contains no instance of 'famous for being famous', and gives Warhol's dates as 6 August 1928 – 22 February 1987 and the 15-minutes line as from a 1968 Stockholm exhibition catalogue.

Charles Godfrey Leland lived 15 August 1824 – 20 March 1903, was an American humorist and folklorist, wrote Hans Breitmann's Ballads (1871) and Aradia, and published Legends of Florence Collected from the People in 1896.

Warhol probably never said 'In the future everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes'; possible originators named include curator Pontus Hultén (in connection with the 1968 Swedish exhibition brochure), photographer Nat Finkelstein and painter Larry Rivers.
A borrowable scan of Daniel J. Boorstin's The Image is hosted at the Internet Archive (1992 Vintage Books printing).
